item.title: This Is the Real Point of College
item.description:
Three cheers for students starting college! They’ve heard doubts about whether it’s worthwhile; they’ve heard Silicon Valley’s claim that A.I. can feed them all the information (and misinformation) they could possibly want; they know college is expensive. Yet right around now, thousands and thousands of them are starting their undergraduate careers with enthusiasm.

Colleges and universities, like almost all institutions, have suffered from a decline in trust, but that isn’t stopping families from New Orleans to Appleton and from Berkeley to Tuscaloosa from gathering their financial and emotional resources to launch their young people toward a memorable educational experience. Parents will cry; kids will check one another out.

Even the Trump administration, which enjoys berating schools (for not protecting Jews or admitting too many Black people or just not promoting its preferred version of American history), has softened its tone for the moment. Last month, the secretary of education took a break from dismantling her department to issue a national call to action, asking college and university leaders to “advance American security interests, deliver academic programs that meet urgent work force needs, and contribute materially to the nation’s prosperity.” Laudable goals to be sure, and nothing to be neutral about, despite the call’s insistence elsewhere on institutional neutrality. But these are not the goals of students.

A significant percentage of first-year students are entering community college, and many of them will be looking for classes that prepare them for jobs in the near term. Nursing, information technology, the electrical trades and education will appeal to many, but the most popular areas of study are in the liberal arts. That’s no surprise because the liberal arts prepares students to pivot in many directions given shifting labor force needs.

And those shifts will be significant. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how tasks are completed almost everywhere. That’s why students at community colleges, like their counterparts at four-year schools, hope to learn to use large language model tools and develop the human capacities for discernment, for making sense of when and how to use the powerful research and analytic powers of A.I. The students are learning specific skills, to be sure, but they are also learning how to add human value to work in a marketplace infatuated with the wonders of automation.

Despite the pressures of a perilous job market, students often use the first semester for exploration. Course catalogs will include titles that baffle recent high school graduates and lead to head-scratching moments for parents and pundits. But this is nothing new. Some schools provide a core curriculum, and despite oft-repeated stories of far-left professors pouring woke doctrine down the throats of naïve youngsters, the writings of Plato, Machiavelli and Mary Shelley remain among the most assigned college readings in America.

Students in my humanities course this fall will begin with Confucius, Aristotle and Aquinas. Very few of my undergrads will major in philosophy, but almost all, I expect, will approach the material with energetic curiosity. They always do. Why? Because they are taking the opportunity to discover who they are as readers, as conversation partners, as people. They are figuring out what kind of work they find fulfilling, what they love to do.

That said, it is essential that students also learn how to get better at the work they’ve signed up for. Discovering one’s passion is not enough. Through vigorous practice, students should learn to work harder and better, so they can go further than they’d thought possible. If they use A.I. to avoid having to work hard, they’ll learn little.

Grade inflation, too, is pernicious, because it signals to young people that they’ve already mastered a task when they’ve really just begun to get the hang of it. Teachers must get over their fear of alienating students by setting high standards, and undergraduates must come to understand that they can do much better than they’ve already done. And they need to learn without undue dependence on technology.

I’ve been teaching college students for over 40 years, and one of the great pleasures for me at the beginning of the school year is seeing students develop friendships in their new surroundings. It may happen in a science lab or on a sports team, or through a discussion begun in class and carried over into the dining hall or the dorm. Every year I meet alumni in ripe old age who are still buddies with (or even married to) people they got to know in the first weeks of school. I’m convinced that there is something about young folks opening themselves to new possibilities in college that sets a durable foundation for long-lasting relationships.

Yes, college is less affordable than it should be; yes, there’s still a long way to go in improving intellectual diversity and pluralism on campus. Yes, it’s all too easy to mock the bombast or simple riotousness of the young. From Thomas Jefferson to Richard Nixon to Donald Trump, people have raised complaints about college students. After all, these students are learning how to practice freedom — the opposite of trying to figure out just how to fit into the world that is being left them.

Today’s students are trying to work out what it means to be decent humans in a world growing more heated, hostile and, sometimes, heartless. We should cheer them on, for their sake and ours.

Michael S. Roth, the president of Wesleyan University, is the author of “The Student: A Short History” and “Safe Enough Spaces: A Pragmatist’s Approach to Inclusion, Free Speech, and Political Correctness on College Campuses.”

item.title: $100 Million Changed Notre Dame’s No-Advertisement Attitude
item.description:
The University of Notre Dame prides itself on a clean, advertisement-free look. Notre Dame Stadium has no corporate sponsors. No billboards wink at the crowd from the sidelines or tunnel entrances. What happens on the field beneath the “Touchdown Jesus” mural is meant to be college football at its purest.

That’s why Notre Dame’s recent decision to add an advertising patch on every student-athlete’s sports jersey has rattled many Fighting Irish faithful.

Starting this year, Notre Dame athletes in all sports will wear the logo of the personal finance company SoFi near the shoulder of their jerseys in a deal worth more than $100 million over the next six years, according a person familiar with the deal who was not authorized to speak publicly about the terms.

The deal is a result of the modern realities of college sports, where top athletes are now compensated for their play. During the 2026-27 school year, athletes could earn $3.78 billion in compensation. Putting together the best teams often requires schools to pay up. A top quarterback could cost a school as much as $5 million, a wide receiver up to $1 million and defensive lineman up to $800,000.

An N.C.A.A. policy adopted in January allowing schools to place up to two sponsorship patches on player uniforms is considered a lifeboat for universities trying to keep up. Louisiana State University, Wisconsin, Ohio State and many more have patch deals.

But Notre Dame?

“The immediate reaction was people weren’t happy and presumed we were selling out by Notre Dame,” said Sean Stires, an evening host at WSBT, a popular sports talk radio station in South Bend and the school’s flagship station.

On the ESPN talk show “First Take,” Chris Russo, popularly known as “Mad Dog,” said football factories like Ohio State cut those kinds of deals, not a program as steeped in history as Notre Dame.

“It’s the Fighting Irish,” said Mr. Russo, whose daughter graduated from the university. “It’s Knute Rockne. It’s 1934. It’s Lou Holtz. It’s everybody.”

Aaron Horvath, Notre Dame’s deputy athletics director, acknowledged that change was hard for some Notre Dame fans and expected pushback. But, he said, schools need to innovate financially in order to keep improving their teams.

“That is a new age of college athletics,” Mr. Horvath said.

For alumni like Brady Quinn, a star quarterback for the Irish from 2003 to 2006, the patches were a necessary step for Notre Dame to continue to be one of the best teams in the sport.

But he also said deep-pocketed donors — citing the $150 million football center named for donors, not corporations — and deep reverence among the fan base for the Notre Dame mystique would force athletic officials to show some restraint in the types of corporate deals they sold.

“If you’re asking are they going to turn into a NASCAR, no, I don’t think the stadium or I don’t think the jerseys or the program will ever turn into that,” Mr. Quinn said.

He said he could see universities finding ways to turn certain logistics, like transportation to games, into sponsorship opportunities. Picture an official airline sponsor of Notre Dame football, or planes with the Notre Dame logo next to the airline’s.

“You’d have to kind of get creative,” he said.

Branded sponsorships have been part of college football for decades. Even before athletes were allowed to profit from the industry, sponsors began paying to name bowl games, stadiums and practice facilities.

Bobby Carpenter, who played at Ohio State in the early 2000s, remembers playing against Notre Dame in the Tostitos Fiesta Bowl and wearing patches with the tortilla chip brand’s logo on them.

“So, you have a bowl patch, but it also has branding to it,” he said. “And no one ever made like a huge deal about that.”

Ohio State, Mr. Carpenter’s alma mater, announced a multiyear jersey patch deal with Chase Bank worth about $17 million just a few days before Notre Dame announced its deal last month. And the whole of the Big 12 Conference signed with Monster Energy for $16 million to be split by all its members.

Many Notre Dame alumni take competitive pride in their deal. Kyle Rudolph, a Notre Dame football alum who made two Pro Bowls during his 12-year N.F.L. career, said the patch fit with Notre Dame’s values.

“You know, you evolve with the time; you hold yourself to a high standard,” he said. Then he laughed a little. “You’re not going to be the Big 12 and give it away for a million bucks a school. I mean, that’s just absolutely ridiculous.”

How much bang will SoFi get with its bucks?

Kelsey Slater, an assistant professor of sports promotion at the University of Nebraska, led a study published this year that tracked people’s eyes as they watched Major League Baseball games on television to see how much attention people gave to teams’ jersey sponsors. The study found that on average viewers spent one second looking at jersey sponsorships. After glancing at them once, they were unlikely to look again.

Still, companies do benefit from their association with sports teams, said Jonathan Jensen, an associate professor at Texas A&M University.

Mr. Jensen, another Notre Dame alum, said Notre Dame’s history was replete with examples of corporate sponsorships that figured prominently. Look no further, he said, than Rockne, who helped build Notre Dame football into a powerhouse in the early 1900s.

This year, Rockne’s remains were returned to a cemetery on the campus. He died in a plane crash in 1931.

“Knute Rockne was the P.T. Barnum of college football,” Mr. Jensen said

Rockne was happy to engage with corporate sponsors. He recruited the car manufacturer Studebaker as one of Notre Dame football’s early sponsors. Then in 1928, Studebaker hired him as a motivational speaker. A few years later, he became the automaker’s manager of sales promotion, all while serving as the school’s head football coach and athletic director.

It’s something Notre Dame’s administrators think about as they plunge into the modern world of college sports.

Mr. Horvath, the deputy athletics director, invoked Rockne’s name to defend the patch. The coaching legend would have considered anything that might make his team “1 percent” better, he said.

“We felt this was a new opportunity to innovate like a Knute Rockne did back in the ’20s,” Mr. Horvath said.

My interviews for this story often turned into really interesting discussions about whether this era of college sports, where players are paid salaries and are generally more empowered, is good or bad for the athletes. The three former players I spoke with all agreed they liked seeing players get paid, especially since some of them won't play professionally and are making more in college than they ever will again. But they also felt nostalgic for their own college days, and a little sad some of today's players have to grow up so much faster.

When I started covering college football, there were no playoffs and you got kicked off the team for accepting free tennis shoes or a tattoo. Now college football players can make as much, sometimes more, than N.F.L. stars. Universities have to come up with money they don’t have. The $100 million patch deal is just the beginning.

item.title: School Is Starting Late. That’s Good for N.Y.C. Summer Camps.
item.description:
New York City public schools are starting later than they have in years past. For some parents, it’s a child care headache, but for day camps, it’s been a boon.

Brooklyn Music Factory in Carroll Gardens has 62 children on the wait list for its final week of camp, for a program that has 42 places at its main space and 18 at a satellite location. Its co-founder and camp director, Peira Moinester, said this was the first time in the camp’s 16-year history that so many parents were checking their place in line.

“It feels particularly heated in terms of people trying to get in the door,” she said.

The seemingly endless summer for city students — who return to class Sept. 10 — is a result of the city teachers’ union contract that includes a post-Labor Day start date with two days for professional development and preparation. (By comparison, in Los Angeles, students were back in public school on Aug. 12.)

Traditional day camps often end in mid-August, either because counselors return to college or staff members pivot to planning for after-school offerings, some camp directors said. And the city’s free summer program, Summer Rising, ended several weeks ago.

For working parents, that has meant taking paid or unpaid time off, relying on screen time, hiring babysitters — or snagging spots at camps staying open into September.

“I feel like this summer, everybody just feels stretched to the ends of what we are capable of managing,” said Julia Blaney, 39, a design director and mother of two living in Brooklyn. She cobbled together child care via day camps and help from her mother and a friend’s teenage son.

She said that when the school calendar was announced, “everybody was in a complete panic.”

Some camps — particularly smaller specialty camps — are offering additional weeks, extra hours and, in some cases, more scholarships. Several smaller camps said they were grateful for the added income, citing high overhead and the strain of running a small business that is in operation for a only few hours per day during the school year.

When Allegra Glinsky, the director of the Brooklyn Dance Conservatory, opened camp registration in early January, several parents mentioned the late school start, she said. Since her two-year-old program is run by professionals who can work right up until the start of the school year, she said she could cover what some parents had referred to as “campless week.”

“They said, ‘Just so you know, this is going to be an issue,’” she recalled them saying, adding that they were ready to sign up.

SKATEYOGI, a camp offering skateboarding lessons, is similarly able to run straight through to the start of school this year. Founded 13 years ago with two Brooklyn locations, the camp generally has greater flexibility for late enrollment since most campers attend for only one week.

The extra week has been a gift, said Kevin Banahan, the co-founder and executive director of the program, which he runs with his partner, Yasuyo Takeo. “We’ve had students, maybe, that would be gone for the summer, but because they’ve got this extra week, they’re able to come and try it out,” Mr. Banahan said. Some of those campers have now committed to signing up for SKATEYOGI’s after-school programming.

Paying for extra days of camp, however, can add to the already significant costs of child care in the city. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has taken several steps to address such concerns; the mayor, with Gov. Kathy Hochul, has expanded free child care to 2-year-olds in some communities, and the city provided some parents with an evening of free babysitting during its Parents’ Night Out program.

Tabitha Decker, 47, of Brooklyn said that her son had attended nine-and-a-half weeks of camp, ranging in cost from $450 to around $900 per week. But Ms. Decker — a member of New Yorkers United for Childcare, an organization that advocates universal child care — sees herself as fortunate compared with many other parents: She can call upon her mother for support and has the financial means to pay for camp.

“Even in the best-case scenario,” she said, “this is a patchwork.”

As one of the NYC parents cobbling together activities for my kids in these final days of summer, I'm in a lot of group chats searching for creative ways to occupy little ones. I was surprised by the number of creative options our reporter found!
